chapter.title: What counts as a good argument

cards.body:
Picture the dinner table. Someone says, "We should ban cars from the city centre." Before anyone answers, the sharpest guest asks a quiet question: what is the claim, and what is holding it up?

That is the one game every guest has played for 2,500 years. **Split what someone says into the claim and the reasons under it**, then check whether the reasons bear the weight. Think of the claim as a tabletop and each reason as a leg.
cards.simpler:
Imagine a dinner table. Someone says, "We should ban cars from the city centre." Before anyone replies, the sharpest guest asks a quiet question: what is being claimed, and what holds it up?

People have played this game for 2,500 years. **Split what someone says into the claim and the reasons under it**, then check whether those reasons can carry the weight. Think of the claim as a tabletop and each reason as a leg.

cards.prompt: Your cousin says over dessert: "Pineapple on pizza is wrong, because my dad never ate it and Italians invented pizza." Which bit is the claim?

whyNot.b: That's a reason, not the claim: it's one leg offered to hold the tabletop up.
whyNot.c: That's a reason too: a fact your cousin hopes will carry the claim.

cards.reteach: The claim is the thing the speaker wants you to accept, the point of the whole sentence. The reasons are what comes after "because". Find the "because" and the claim is usually sitting just in front of it.

cards.title: Claim and reasons
cards.body:
An *argument* in philosophy is not a fight. It is a claim plus the reasons given for it. The claim is what you are asked to accept. The reasons are what is meant to make you accept it.

Most opinions arrive glued together: "Remote work is better, people get more done and nobody misses the commute." Pull it apart. Claim: remote work is better. Reasons: more gets done, no commute.

Three words do most of the finding: *because*, *so* and *therefore*. Whatever follows "because" is a reason. Whatever follows "so" or "therefore" is the claim. **Find the because.**
cards.simpler:
In philosophy, an argument is not a fight. It is a claim plus the reasons for it. The claim is what you are asked to accept.

Opinions arrive stuck together: "Remote work is better, people get more done and nobody misses the commute." Pull it apart. Claim: remote work is better. Reasons: more done, no commute.

Three words help: because, so and therefore. After "because" comes a reason. After "so" or "therefore" comes the claim. **Find the because.**

cards.title: The flat in Lisbon
cards.body:
Ana wants to move to Lisbon. Her reason, said over dinner: "The weather is great, so I'll be happier there." Her brother Rui does not argue about the weather. He asks whether the sun is doing any work: Ana has lived in sunny Seville for 3 years and spends most of it indoors complaining about the heat.

**The reason is true. It just does not hold the claim up.** Ana moves anyway.
cards.simpler:
Ana wants to move to Lisbon. Over dinner she gives her reason: "The weather is great, so I'll be happier there." Her brother Rui does not argue about the weather. He asks whether the sunshine is really doing anything. Ana has lived in sunny Seville for 3 years and spends most of her time indoors complaining about the heat.

**The reason is true. It just does not hold the claim up.** Ana moves anyway.

cards.prompt: Marcus says: "This phone is the best one on the market, because it's the one I bought." What is the problem with his argument?

options.text: The reason is true but does not hold up the claim
There is no claim, only a reason

whyNot.a: That's a verdict on the tabletop, not a check of the legs: we have not tested whether the phone is best, only whether his reason gets us there.
whyNot.c: "The best one on the market" is the claim: the thing Marcus wants you to accept.

cards.reteach: Imagine the reason is completely true: Marcus did buy this phone. Does that force the claim to be true, that it is the best on the market? No. The reason is a real leg, but it is standing nowhere near the table.

cards.title: Do the legs reach the table?
cards.body:
There are two separate questions. Is each reason true? And, if it is true, does it actually get you to the claim? A reason can pass the first and fail the second. Ana's sunshine was real. It just was not connected to her happiness.

So the test is not "do I agree?". The test is: imagine the reason is fully true. Does the claim now have to be true too? If you can picture the reason true and the claim still false, there is a *gap*: a missing step the speaker has not said out loud.

**A true reason can still leave a gap.** Philosophers spend most of the dinner pointing at gaps.
cards.simpler:
Ask two questions. Is each reason true? And if so, does it get you to the claim? Ana's sunshine was real, but it had nothing to do with her happiness.

The test is not "do I agree?" Pretend the reason is fully true. Must the claim be true too? If the reason can be true while the claim stays false, there is a gap: a step nobody said out loud.

**A true reason can still leave a gap.**

cards.body:
Priya hears, "We should raise the parking fee, because the car park is always full." She hates the idea of a higher fee, so she says "bad argument" and moves on. But she never checked the legs. She judged the tabletop because she did not like it.

Spot it in yourself with one question: **did I find the gap, or do I just dislike the claim?** Those are different things, and only the first one counts.
cards.simpler:
Priya hears, "We should raise the parking fee, because the car park is always full." She hates the idea of paying more, so she says "bad argument" and moves on. But she never checked the legs. She judged the tabletop because she did not like it.

Catch yourself with one question: **did I find the gap, or do I just dislike the claim?** Those are two different things, and only the first one counts.

cards.prompt: Which question tests whether a reason really holds up a claim?

options.text: Do I agree with the claim?
If the reason were fully true, could the claim still be false?

whyNot.a: That's your opinion of the tabletop, not a test of the legs: Priya's mistake.
whyNot.b: That's about who is talking, not whether the reason reaches the claim: experts leave gaps too.

cards.reteach: Picture the reason as completely true. Then ask if the claim could still be false anyway. If yes, the reason is not carrying the claim, however true it is. That one question is the whole test.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every opinion is a claim resting on reasons, and you find the join by looking for the word "because". **A good argument is one where, if the reasons are true, the claim cannot be false**; the gap between them is where philosophers live.
cards.simpler: Every opinion is a claim resting on reasons. You find the join by looking for the word "because". Think of it as a table: the claim on top, the reasons as legs. **A good argument is one where, if the reasons are true, the claim cannot be false.** The gap between reasons and claim is where philosophers do their work.

cards.body: Tonight, pick one opinion from a group chat or a headline. Write it as "Claim: ... because: ...". Then ask: **could the because be true and the claim still false?**
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick one opinion from a group chat or a news headline. Write it down as "Claim: ... because: ...". Then ask yourself one thing: **could the because be true and the claim still false?** If yes, you have found a gap. That is the whole game.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now split any opinion into its claim and its reasons, and say whether the reasons actually hold it up.
